summary:
Nepal criminalises no conduct on the basis of gender identity or gender expression. Same-sex acts have been legal since the Supreme Court's December 2007 judgment in Sunil Babu Pant v. Nepal Government, which held that homosexuality is not 'unnatural'. The Criminal Codes Act 2017, which replaced the 1963 Muluki Ain, still lists 'unnatural sex' on its face and must be read in light of that ruling; the Muluki Ain criminalised 'unnatural sexual intercourse' with up to one year's imprisonment, and LGBTQI+ Nepalis were arrested under it. The age of consent is 18 regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition rests on the 2007 Supreme Court ruling recognising the right to self-determined name and gender markers, and a third-gender category has been available on official documents by self-declaration. Government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male and female marker changes lagged, so the country's progressive reputation has outrun its policy. Changing markers to female or male has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations, including intrusive post-operative genital exams. In August 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed more than 50 lawsuits since 2021. Human Rights Watch called on the government in February 2024 to create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure for transgender and third-gender people to obtain official documents, an intervention that illustrates the absence of a straightforward document-change process; a Kathmandu trans woman holds a 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender. A civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition, the Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078, was published in October 2021 by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi through the Asia Pacific Transgender Network. Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective assessed in 2020 that an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community.

Judicial recognition of foreign same-sex marriages exists: Suman Pant's Supreme Court case set a precedent for same-sex spousal visas. On 28 June 2023 Justice Til Prasad Shrestha issued an interim order directing the government to 'temporarily register' marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities, and the full bench has yet to deliver a final verdict. In April 2024 the National ID and Civil Registration Department instructed local authorities to enter same-sex marriages into a separate register. Temporary registration grants no equal rights: same-sex couples cannot inherit property, receive tax subsidies, make spousal medical decisions or adopt children, and certificates label them 'groom and bride'. The first marriage of a trans woman and a cisgender man took place in November 2023, and as of June 2025 Blue Diamond Society counted at least 17 documented queer marriages. Implementation is inconsistent: the Kathmandu District Court rejected a registration in July 2023, and compliance by local governments is unknown.

A November 2024 Kathmandu Post feature on Janakpur reported that trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. Transgender Nepalis face severe gender-based violence and interrupted education, especially in rural areas.

The first gender-affirming surgery in Nepal was performed in June 2025 at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, which has since established a Gender Affirming Clinic. Hormone replacement therapy and sex reassignment surgery remain hard to reach: a six-month hormone supply costs 4,500 rupees, providers are few, and many trans Nepalis take hormones without medical supervision because of stigma. Some travel to India and Thailand for surgery.

On 30 October 2024 the Aamul Paribartan Nagarik Party held a protest rally opposing homosexuality and LGBTQ rights, with Mitini Nepal's executive director noting that anti-LGBTQ sentiments are gaining momentum in Nepal and South Asia. In April 2026 newly elected Prime Minister Balen Shah faced LGBTQ community criticism over a YouTube rap video containing derogatory and homophobic hate speech; after demands for an apology, his supporters markedly increased derogatory comments, hate speech and death threats against the community.
tangentialFactors:
The Communist Party of Nepal-Maoist made homophobic statements during the Civil War, describing homosexuality as 'a production of capitalism' and LGBT people as 'social pollutants'.

Media representation of LGBT people has historically been negative or comic relief, with caricatures of transgender people, gay people and lesbians, though Highway (2012) and Soongava (2012) offered positive depictions. Nepali media has been criticised for forcefully using 'third gender' to describe trans men and trans women. Some observers accused media and activists of pinkwashing and spreading disinformation about same-sex marriage and LGBT rights.

Annual pride events include the Nepal Pride Parade, held since 2019, and Queer Womxn Pride and the Trans Pride Parade, held since 2020.

A 2015 SIT Study Abroad study found that despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.
localsOnly:
The Education Board has implemented information about sexual and gender diversity in the curriculum for grades 7 to 9 (ages 13 to 15), making Nepal the second Asian country after Mongolia to do so, and universities offer courses on LGBT issues. Many LGBT children nonetheless face discrimination and leave school because of threats, bullying and neglect by fellow students and teachers.

During the 2011 census, some enumerators demanded that a child be stripped when parents listed them as 'third gender'.

Conversion therapy is practised, including treatment in rehabilitation centres and traditional exorcism by family members. Lesbian couples are denied IVF, and research and healthcare addressing LGBT Nepalis' needs are severely lacking.

A drop-in centre with free HIV testing operates in Kathmandu through the Blue Diamond Society, which has more than 50 branches; Mitini Nepal, Parichaya Samaj and Sahaayam Nepal also provide resources. Queer Youth Group has filed writ petitions at the Supreme Court demanding legal recognition of gender identity and has advocated for the citizenship bill.

UNDP has recommended that transgender and intersex students be given access to safe toilets and bathroom facilities.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Supreme Court's full bench has not delivered a final verdict on the interim order directing temporary registration of marriages of non-traditional couples and sexual minorities; whether local governments comply with the April 2024 instruction to record such marriages in a separate register is not sourced.

Whether the August 2024 ruling requiring recognition of a trans woman as a woman on all documents without medical verification has changed practice at document-issuing offices nationally is not established by the sources.

The number of providers offering hormone therapy or gender-affirming surgery in Nepal is not quantified beyond the statement that providers are few.
